mcqs.question: In a stack trace, what does the "throw site" tell you that the trace alone cannot?
options: The exact line where the exception was raised, but not why the bad value existed in the first place
The complete root cause of the bug, including upstream data issues
Which team owns the code that needs to be fixed
Whether the bug is reproducible on demand
mcqs.explanation: The throw site pinpoints where the program noticed the failure, which is valuable but not the whole story — a NoneType error at a multiplication doesn't explain why an upstream step produced an item with a None price. That upstream reasoning is the hypothesis you still have to build.

mcqs.question: A 40-frame stack trace has only 3 frames from your own application, the rest from libraries and the framework. Where should you focus first?
options: The very last frame at the bottom of the trace, regardless of whose code it is
The library frame that appears most often across the trace
The first application-code frame you hit walking out from the throw site
The framework's request-dispatch frame, since it started the call chain
mcqs.explanation: Library and framework code is usually well-tested and doing what it was told, so the bug or bad assumption almost always lives in the first frame that's your own code, found by walking outward from the throw site — not by reading top to bottom or by frame frequency.

mcqs.question: A trace shows "OrderLookupError: order lookup failed" caused by "QueryTimeoutException" caused by "SocketTimeoutException: connect timed out". Where should investigation focus?
options: On the top-level OrderLookupError message alone, since it names the failing operation
On the innermost cause, SocketTimeoutException — the actual failure the outer exceptions merely wrapped with context
Equally on all three exceptions, since each is equally likely to be the bug
On QueryTimeoutException, since it's the middle layer and usually the source
mcqs.explanation: The innermost exception is the real failure; outer exceptions just add context about what the caller was attempting. Reading only the top-level message and stopping there is exactly how people spend time looking for an application bug when the actual issue is a database connection timing out.

mcqs.question: A team needs to answer "how many order failures had reason=timeout in the last hour, across all regions" from logs spanning many services. What does that require?
options: Structured log fields that can be filtered and aggregated, not free-text messages needing regex across inconsistent wording
Setting every log line to error level so nothing is missed
A single service consolidating all logging so there's only one log file to search
Switching all logs to debug level for maximum detail
mcqs.explanation: This kind of cross-service aggregation is exactly what structured fields (event, reason, region) are for — a query on real fields instead of a regex over free text that three teams likely phrased three different ways. Log level and consolidating services don't solve the querying problem.

mcqs.question: Why is a correlation ID minted once at the edge (gateway/load balancer) rather than by each service independently?
options: So that log storage costs less per service
So that only the gateway needs to write any logs at all
Because individual services aren't allowed to generate their own identifiers
So every downstream hop for one request shares the same identifier, letting all its log lines be reconstructed with a single query regardless of timing
mcqs.explanation: Minting once at the edge and propagating it through headers and queue payloads is what lets one request's full journey be pulled with a single filter, even across async hops that happen minutes apart. If each service generated its own ID independently, there'd be nothing tying the pieces together.

mcqs.question: A service logs `log.error(f"failed: {request}")` on any handler error. What's the structural fix for the risk this creates?
options: Ask every engineer to remember to manually scrub sensitive fields before each log call
Disable error-level logging in production entirely
Redact or allowlist fields at the logging layer itself, so sensitive values can't leak even if a call site is careless
Move all logs to a separate service with the same access controls as the primary datastore
mcqs.explanation: Relying on individual engineers to remember to scrub every log call doesn't scale and fails the moment someone forgets — the fix is structural, redacting or allowlisting at the logging layer so a careless log.error(request) can't leak a token. Disabling error logs loses real signal, and logs typically do have looser access than primary datastores, which is the actual problem.
